processing: Its famous Virgin White is cut from the bush with scissors and, by the owner's account, never touched by hand; as with white tea generally it is simply withered and dried.
harvest_season: Output is tiny; little is documented about a specific picking season.
appearance_dry: As with other bud white teas, pale silvery buds, downy and unbroken.
appearance_liquor: As with other bud whites, very pale straw and clear.
appearance_wet: Soft, plump, pale buds, typical of the style.
taste_profile: Detailed independent tasting records are scarce; expect what is typical of bud white tea, gentle, faintly sweet and softly floral.

brewing.notes: Cool water and generous time, as with other bud whites. Boiling water flattens it.

vintage_note: Sold in very small quantities at a high price; one trade report gives about 10 kg a year. It has been stocked by Mariage Frères in Paris. As with fresh white tea, buy recent stock and ask for the production date.
description:
Handunugoda is a family-owned estate of about 200 acres at Ahangama on Sri Lanka's south coast, run by the tea man Malinga Herman Gunaratne. It stands apart from the hill-country image of Ceylon tea, sitting in low country near the sea, and it is known above all for one white tea.

That tea, Herman Virgin White, is cut with scissors and handled without bare hands. Gunaratne says that to the best of his knowledge it is the only tea in the world untouched by hand; that is his own claim. The picking is very slow: one trade report puts a plucker's day at 160 grams of leaf, against a general 30 kilos.

The style follows the bud-white pattern, so brew it cool and long, with water around 80°C. Claims about high antioxidant content come from the owner himself, so don't buy it for that reason.

You are paying for scarcity and a story as much as for the cup. A trade report once put it at US$1,500 per kilo. Compare it with a fresh Bai Hao Yin Zhen and decide for yourself.
history:
The inspiration is a legend: the Chinese story of tea cut with golden scissors for emperors. Gunaratne says he heard the story from a British colleague and set out to make his own version.

One profile says the tea was ready for market in 2009.
